sentences.text: Thirty sailors ran back and forth across a brand-new warship.
After the third run, the admiral stopped the test, and the ship sailed anyway.
It's 1628 in Stockholm.
The king, away at war, orders seventy-two heavy cannons for his new warship, the Vasa.
So it gets two decks of guns, stacked high above the water, and hundreds of carvings.
But every run rocks it harder.
The admiral wishes the king were home.
The king's letters say: get her to sea.
On August tenth, a huge crowd watches four sails go up.
A gust tips the Vasa over.
It rights itself.
Then a second gust pushes the lower gun ports under the water.
The gun deck floods, and thirteen hundred meters out, in front of everyone, the Vasa sinks.
About thirty people die.
The inquiry punishes no one.
Only God knows, one builder says.
You see, a ship stays upright like a weighted toy: heavy at the bottom, light at the top.
The Vasa was the opposite.
Its bronze cannons sat high on two decks, over just 120 tons of stone.
It needed about twice as much, but more weight would push the lower gun ports down to the waterline.
So when thirty men ran across the deck, the ship was already warning them.
In 1961, they raised it from the mud, almost whole.
It sits in Stockholm today, never sailing again.
